assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, with the magic-wavelength idea and its realisation, brought atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level. This is a precision-measurement achievement of the kind I trust most: a clean physical idea, quantitatively controlled, that opens tests of fundamental constants, relativistic redshift at millimetre scales and a possible redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated early Sr clocks; Ye's group pushed the systematic uncertainty and stability to record levels and measured gravitational redshift across a sample. Two laureates is a natural fit. Other groups (e.g. ion-clock and Yb-lattice work) contributed, but the credited pair has the decisive lineage.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced and surpassed by many independent laboratories (Sr, Yb, Hg); comparisons between clocks are routine. The interpretation is very stable. Recognition is timely as redefinition of the SI second is being prepared.
uncertainties: Fair weighting between the Katori idea and the Ye-group performance records is not fully settled in my mind.
The ion-clock and frequency-comb contributions are partly recognised by earlier prizes, so overlap needs care.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices gave a controllable realisation of Hubbard-type models, with the superfluid to Mott-insulator transition as the signature result, and now allow quantum simulation of many-body physics with single-site resolution. It reveals genuinely new access to quantum matter, and many-body theory is close to my own field.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch, Cirac and collaborators) supplied the proposal for Hubbard models with cold atoms; Greiner and Bloch realised the Mott transition; Esslinger did fermionic realisations; Cirac is a major theorist. Five credited names exceed what the prize allows, so any trio leaves out decisive people. I pick one theorist and two experimentalists, but the choice is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: a large community, repeated independent confirmation, and quantitative theory-experiment agreement. The field is arguably overdue for recognition, though the prize partly overlaps with the 2001 BEC and 2012 cold-atom prizes.
uncertainties: Which three of Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Zoller and Cirac should be chosen is genuinely unresolved.
Whether the headline results are quantum simulation or the underlying cooling and trapping techniques already recognised.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The observation of the Higgs boson completed the Standard Model and confirmed the mechanism recognised in 2013. It is an unquestionably important discovery, the most significant in particle physics in decades, though I defer to colleagues on particle physics.
assessment.attribution: The theory was credited in 2013. For the experimental discovery, the decisive roles were in conceiving and leading ATLAS and CMS; Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni are named, and Virdee is a fourth credited name who cannot be included under the three-person limit. Collaboration-scale attribution is inherently difficult and the Committee has long been reluctant to prize collaborations.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by two experiments and with growing precision on couplings; fully mature and stable. Timing is acceptable, with the main obstacle being the attribution structure rather than the science.
uncertainties: Whether the statutes and committee tradition can accommodate crediting individuals for a collaboration discovery.
Omitting Tejinder Virdee leaves an asymmetric credit between ATLAS and CMS.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapping, cooling and precision spectroscopy of antihydrogen and antiprotons test CPT symmetry and antimatter gravity with exquisite precision. The questions are fundamental and the techniques are atomic-physics at its best, which appeals to me.
assessment.attribution: Gabrielse developed trapping of antiprotons, positrons and high-precision single-particle measurements; Hangst led ALPHA, which trapped and spectroscopically probed antihydrogen. Both are clearly decisive, though other collaborations (ATRAP, ASACUSA, AEgIS, GBAR) overlap and Gabrielse's work spans both traps.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature, with ALPHA and ATRAP results reproduced in spirit, but the key hoped-for finding of a violation has not appeared, so the case rests on technique and precision rather than a new effect. Stable but could mature further.
uncertainties: Absence of a symmetry-breaking result may count against recognition at this time.
Relative contributions of the ALPHA, ATRAP and ASACUSA collaborations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Z2 topological insulator and quantum spin Hall effect opened a vast field of topological quantum matter, with a clear theoretical idea and a concrete experimental confirmation in HgTe. It is original and very influential, although I defer to condensed-matter colleagues on the relative standing within that field.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the theory of the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall effect in graphene. The HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and its experimental observation by Molenkamp's group are decisive but split across people, and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang are not in the credited list. Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a coherent configuration, though not clearly complete.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and 3D materials via ARPES, with broad independent verification. The 2016 prize recognised topological phase transitions in a related but distinct domain.
uncertainties: The omission of the HgTe theory proposers from the credited names.
Kane-Mele's graphene prediction is not experimentally realised at observable gaps, so the pairing with the HgTe experiment is a compound story.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics achieves strong coupling of a superconducting artificial atom to a single microwave photon, with the dispersive readout that underpins superconducting qubits. It is an elegant realisation of cavity QED concepts in a new regime and opened a major platform.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 theory proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the Yale experiment (Wallraff et al.) are the decisive items; Wallraff is not on the credited list. Schoelkopf, Girvin and Blais are plausible, though I would like to see Wallraff considered. Prior prize recognition of circuit quantum tunnelling (2025) and of cavity QED (2012) overlaps.
assessment.maturity: Replicated widely in many laboratories and underlies current quantum processors; stable. Possibly slightly premature for a basic-science prize given the recent 2025 award in a neighbouring area.
uncertainties: Recognition of the 2025 prize may reduce appetite for a further superconducting-circuit award soon.
Allocation between theory (Blais, Girvin) and experiment (Schoelkopf) credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and Berry's phase reveal that geometric and topological structure shapes quantum mechanics, and they connect to many subfields from molecular dynamics to topological matter. It speaks directly to the fundamental understanding of quantum mechanics that I value.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm (1959) predicted the effect; David Bohm has died, so credit would pass to Aharonov. Berry (1984) introduced the geometric phase, with earlier related work by Pancharatnam. Two living candidates fit, but the pairing joins two distinct discoveries.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally confirmed (Tonomura, Chambers) and the geometric phase observed in many systems; the concepts are textbook. The age of the discovery is a point of caution about timeliness, not about maturity.
uncertainties: Whether Aharonov-Bohm and Berry phase are one discovery or two, and whether combining them is coherent.
Bohm's death and the Pancharatnam and Longuet-Higgins precedence for geometric phases.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The recollision model explains high-harmonic generation and is the conceptual base of attosecond science. I know this area well and I value its physical clarity, but the 2023 prize already recognised the experimental attosecond methods, so a further award needs a distinct core discovery.
assessment.attribution: Corkum (1993) gave the three-step picture; Schafer, Kulander and collaborators gave the same recollision physics at the time; Lewenstein et al. provided the quantum strong-field theory. Because of my close collaborators in this area I would approach this ranking cautiously. Krausz and L'Huillier's 2023 award does not cover the recollision model, but overlap is real.
assessment.maturity: The model is confirmed in many experiments including rescattering, imaging and attosecond pulses; stable. Timeliness is arguable given the 2023 award.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2023 prize may make a second award in the same area unlikely.
My professional proximity to this field may bias my assessment; I have placed it low for that reason.
